html:
The standard silver coin of Rome, first struck around 211 BCE during the Second Punic War. Its name means "containing ten", since it was first worth ten bronze asses.

For about four and a half centuries it was the everyday money of the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire. Soldiers' pay, wages and taxes were counted in denarii. The coins carried portraits and messages, and Julius Caesar was the first living Roman to put his own face on one.

Emperors slowly cut its silver content to pay their armies. By the 200s CE it was mostly base metal and prices soared. It was pushed aside by the antoninianus and finally by Constantine's gold solidus. Roman coins travelled as far as south India in the spice trade. The name lives on in the Arabic dinar and in the "d" that stood for the penny in old British money.
